headline: Restored Cheshire Wetland Becomes Haven for Rare Birds
meta_description: A restored wetland near Warrington now hosts almost two-thirds of the UK's breeding black-necked grebes, the country's rarest breeding birds.
summary_short: Woolston Eyes, once a dumping ground, is now home to nearly two-thirds of Britain's breeding black-necked grebes—the largest colony in the country.
body:
A restored wetland in Cheshire is now home to almost two-thirds of the UK's breeding black-necked grebes, one of the country's rarest breeding birds. Woolston Eyes, located near Warrington, has become the site of the country's largest colony of the species.

The transformation is remarkable given the site's troubled past. The wetland was previously used as a dumping ground for dredging material from the Manchester Ship Canal—a polluted legacy that made its ecological recovery seem unlikely. Yet restoration efforts have succeeded in creating ideal habitat for these elusive birds.

Black-necked grebes are recognised by their distinctive golden facial tufts and remain uncommon across the UK, with an average of about 55 breeding pairs recorded annually. That Woolston Eyes now hosts nearly two-thirds of this precious population underscores both the rarity of the species and the power of wetland restoration to reverse environmental damage and support wildlife.
